issues.legal_issue: A tax on aggregate net wealth that includes land is distinct from a tax imposed directly on lands and buildings as separate units.
material_facts: The challenged central law imposed tax on an assessee’s net wealth, calculated by aggregating assets and deducting debts.
The amendment brought agricultural land into the assets included in that calculation.
The value of land was included as one component of the assessee’s aggregate wealth, rather than being taxed directly as a separate unit of property.
issues.conclusion: The amended wealth tax was not a tax on lands and buildings within the State legislative field.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 246 and Entry 49 of List II, a tax on lands and buildings is directly imposed on those properties as units and is not concerned with the owner’s total assets or debts. A tax on aggregate net wealth is a personal tax on the assessee and is conceptually distinct. The Court relied on Sudhir Chandra Nawn v. Wealth Tax Officer, Assistant Commissioner of Urban Land Tax v. Buckingham & Carnatic Co. Ltd., and Gift Tax Officer v. Nazareth. It also cautioned, relying on Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for Ontario and Attorney-General for Alberta v. Attorney-General for Canada, that legislation is invalid if its true effect is to invade the State field.

predicates.wealth_tax_competence_challenge: A taxpayer challenges a central wealth-tax law on the ground that the legislature lacked competence to enact it.
predicates.tax_on_aggregate_net_wealth: The law calculates tax by aggregating an assessee’s assets and deducting debts.
predicates.land_not_taxed_as_a_separate_unit: The law includes land only as a component of aggregate wealth and does not impose tax directly on each parcel as a separate unit.

issues.definition: When a challenged wealth tax is based on aggregate net wealth and land is not taxed as a separate unit, the levy is not a tax directly on property.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament’s residuary legislative power covers a tax not assigned to the State or Concurrent Lists even when the taxed asset is excluded from a specified Union List entry.
material_facts: The amendment included agricultural land in the assets used to calculate wealth tax.
The Court held that the amended levy was not a tax on lands and buildings under Entry 49 of List II.
The Constitution’s specified Union tax entry concerning capital value of assets excluded agricultural land.
The Court found no assignment of the tax at issue to the State or Concurrent Lists.
issues.conclusion: Parliament had legislative competence under Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I to include agricultural land in the wealth-tax calculation, and the amendment was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 246 and 248, read with Entry 97 of List I, give Parliament residuary power over matters and taxes not assigned to the State or Concurrent Lists. The legislative lists demarcate fields; an exclusion in a specified Union entry does not, by itself, bar Parliament from legislating under its residuary power. The Court relied on The Governor-General in Council v. The Raleigh Investment Co. and Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia v. Union of India on the function of legislative entries, and on Gift Tax Officer v. Nazareth, Subramanyan Chettiar v. Muttuswami Goundan, State of Bombay v. Narothamdas Jethabhai, and In re The Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada concerning residuary and supplementary legislative powers.

predicates.central_law_competence_challenge: A person challenges a central law on the ground that the legislature lacked competence to enact it.
predicates.tax_not_assigned_to_state_or_concurrent_: The tax imposed by the law is not assigned to either the State or Concurrent legislative fields.
predicates.asset_excluded_from_a_specific_union_ent: The law concerns an asset expressly excluded from a specified Union legislative entry.

issues.definition: If a challenged central law concerns a tax outside the State and Concurrent fields, an asset’s exclusion from a specified Union entry does not prevent Parliament from legislating residually.
